units.title: Unit 03 — Parts of the body
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 3, printed pp. 12–13 (PDF pp. 13–14); original learning examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)
learningObjectives: Identify major parts of the head, face, arms, legs, torso, and internal body, and associate them with simple functions.
Use the irregular plurals tooth/teeth and foot/feet and treat hair as usually uncountable when referring to all the hair on a person’s head.
Pronounce eye, knee, stomach, heart, blood, foot, and tooth; recognize the silent initial k in knee and final b in thumb.
Use possessive determiners with body parts, such as my arm, her hair, and his shoulder, rather than the in ordinary personal contexts.
Recognize the illustrated compound nouns armchair, football, lipstick, hairbrush, headscarf, and handbag.
Identify body parts from descriptions, spelling clues, or pictures and correct errors involving plurals and possessives.

items.example: Her hair is very long.
items.note: Hair is usually uncountable when referring to all the hair on a person’s head: her hair is long, not her hairs are long. A single strand can be a hair.

items.example: Close your eyes, please.
items.note: Eye sounds like the pronoun I.

items.example: My nose is cold.
I need to brush my teeth.
items.note: Irregular plural: tooth → teeth. The final /θ/ is voiceless; place the tongue lightly between the teeth.

items.example: He has small ears.
Open your mouth, please.
Her lips are dry.
My neck hurts today.
She put her bag on her shoulder.
His nails are clean.
I hurt my thumb.
items.note: The final b is silent.

items.example: Point with your finger.
items.note: A finger is part of the hand; a toe is part of the foot. The first syllable of finger is stressed.

items.example: Wash your hands before eating.
Raise your right arm.
My legs feel tired.
She hurt her knee while running.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: My left foot hurts.
items.note: Irregular plural: foot → feet. The vowel /ʊ/ differs from /uː/ in food; this contrast is an additional pronunciation tip.

items.example: I have five toes on each foot.
He felt pain in his chest.
I have a pain in my side.
My stomach hurts after lunch.
items.note: The ch is pronounced /k/.

items.example: My back hurts from sitting all day.
The belt goes around your waist.
Protect your skin from the sun.
She put her hands on her hips.
Your heart beats faster when you run.
The brain controls the body.
The nurse took a blood sample.
items.note: The vowel is /ʌ/, not /uː/.

items.example: He turned his head to look at the door.
items.note: Head refers to the whole head; face is the front part. Both terms appear in the unit headings and exercises.

items.example: She washed her face before breakfast.
items.note: Use a possessive with body parts in personal contexts: wash your face, not wash the face.

items.example: Exercise is good for your body.
items.note: Plural: bodies /ˈbɒdiz/.

items.example: My little brother has two new teeth.
items.note: Irregular plural: tooth → teeth, not tooths.

items.example: My feet are cold after the walk.
items.note: Irregular plural: foot → feet, not foots.

items.example: There is a comfortable armchair beside the window.
items.note: A compound noun formed from arm + chair; illustrated in Exercise 3.4.

items.example: The children played football in the garden.
items.note: A compound noun formed from foot + ball; illustrated in Exercise 3.4.

items.example: She put on some red lipstick for the party.
items.note: A compound noun formed from lip + stick; illustrated in Exercise 3.4.

items.example: I keep my hairbrush in the bathroom.
items.note: A compound noun formed from hair + brush. A brush is different from a comb.

items.example: She wears a blue headscarf in winter.
items.note: A compound noun formed from head + scarf; illustrated in Exercise 3.4.

items.example: She put her phone in her handbag.
items.note: A compound noun formed from hand + bag. Handbag also occurs in Unit 04.

items.example: I wash my hair after swimming.
items.note: In everyday contexts, use a possessive such as my, your, his, or her before hair. When hair means the hair on a person’s head collectively, it is usually uncountable.

items.word: have a pain in my leg
items.example: I have a pain in my leg after running.
items.note: A common body-part construction uses a possessive: a pain in my leg, not a pain in the leg when referring to your own leg.

items.example: Do you know your blood type?
items.note: Exercise 3.2 introduces blood type with the categories A, B, AB, and O. Blood group is also common in British English.

units.title: Unit 04 — Clothes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 4, printed pp. 14–15 (PDF pp. 15–16); original learning examples.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)
learningObjectives: Name the clothes, accessories, and footwear illustrated in the unit and describe them in original sentences.
Use plural agreement with clothing words such as trousers, jeans, tights, glasses, and pyjamas.
Use a pair of with clothing and accessories normally expressed as plural nouns.
Describe what people wear with wear, be wearing, and have (got) ... on; distinguish wearing clothes from carrying objects.
Distinguish getting dressed or undressed from putting on or taking off individual items; place object pronouns correctly in put it on and take them off.
Identify which body parts different items are worn on and write short descriptions of everyday clothing.

items.example: He put on a hat before going outside.
I wear a warm coat when it is cold.
This jacket has two pockets.
She wore a red scarf around her neck.
I always wear gloves in winter.
items.note: Singular: glove; plural: gloves.

items.example: His shoes are under the bed.
items.note: Singular: shoe; plural: shoes.

items.example: She wears trainers when she goes running.
items.note: British English: trainers. American English: sneakers.

items.example: His boots are wet after the walk.
items.note: Singular: boot; plural: boots.

items.example: He wore a dark suit to the interview.
items.note: A suit is a coordinated set of formal clothes, usually a jacket and trousers or a skirt.

items.example: I need a clean pair of socks.
items.note: Singular: sock; plural: socks.

items.example: Her skirt is green.
He wears a tie at work.
I bought a blue T-shirt yesterday.
My watch is on the desk.
items.note: Here watch is a noun meaning a timepiece worn on the wrist. It is also a verb meaning to look at something for a period of time.

items.example: She is wearing a white shirt.
items.note: A shirt and a T-shirt are different garments. A shirt often has a collar and buttons.

items.example: This dress is perfect for summer.
items.note: As a noun, a dress is a garment; as a verb, dress means to put clothes on.

items.example: She wears a silver ring.
My trousers are too loose, so I need a belt.
That sweater looks very warm.
items.note: A sweater is a knitted upper-body garment. Jumper is a common British English term for a similar garment.

items.example: Put on your jumper; it is cold outside.
items.note: In British English, a jumper is a sweater. In American English, jumper can refer to a different type of garment.

items.example: These trousers are too long.
items.note: This clothing noun normally takes a plural verb: these trousers are, not this trousers is.

items.example: My jeans are black.
items.note: Use plural agreement: my jeans are blue. To refer to one garment, say a pair of jeans.

items.example: His shorts are blue.
items.note: This clothing noun normally takes a plural verb: these shorts are. One garment is a pair of shorts.

items.example: These tights are new.
items.note: In British English, tights normally takes a plural verb even when referring to a single garment.

items.example: Your glasses are on the table.
items.note: Eyewear takes a plural verb: my glasses are new. One item is a pair of glasses. Glass can also mean the material or a drinking vessel.

items.example: My pyjamas are comfortable.
items.note: British spelling: pyjamas; American spelling: pajamas. Use a plural verb: my pyjamas are clean.

items.example: These sunglasses are very useful in summer.
items.note: Use a plural verb: these sunglasses are dark. One item is a pair of sunglasses.

items.pt: um par de; uma peça de (para certas roupas no plural)
items.example: I bought a pair of trousers today.
items.note: Use a pair of trousers, jeans, shorts, or glasses. The garment is grammatically plural, but a pair is singular: this pair is new.

items.example: She wears glasses when she reads.
items.note: Use wear for clothes or accessories that are on the body. Contrast carry for objects such as a suitcase.

items.example: He carries a bag to work every day.
items.note: Use carry for an object that you take with you, such as a bag or an umbrella; wear describes clothes and accessories on the body.

items.example: I get dressed after my shower.
items.note: Get dressed describes the process of putting your clothes on. Be dressed describes the resulting state.

items.pt: vestir; colocar uma peça de roupa
items.example: Please put on your coat before you go out.
items.note: Put on refers to the action of dressing in an item: put on your coat or put your coat on. With a pronoun, use put it on.

items.example: The children get undressed before their bath.
items.note: Get undressed is the opposite of get dressed.

items.pt: tirar uma peça de roupa ou acessório
items.example: Take off your shoes at the door.
items.note: Take off is the opposite of put on for clothes. Say take it off or take them off, not take off it. Do not confuse it with put off.

items.pt: estar usando; estar com o casaco vestido
items.example: She has got a blue jacket on today.
items.note: A natural alternative to be wearing: She has got a coat on. The clothing noun comes between got and on.

items.example: He is wearing a white shirt today.
items.note: Use the continuous form to describe clothes worn at a particular moment: she is wearing a jacket.

items.example: My uncle wears glasses for reading.
items.note: Say wear glasses when they are on your face; carry glasses means taking them somewhere, not necessarily wearing them.

items.example: She is carrying a small suitcase.
items.note: Carrying is the -ing form of carry. Compare she is carrying a bag with she is wearing a coat.

items.example: She carries a bag with her books.
items.note: In the unit’s basic contrast, a person carries a bag but wears clothes.

items.example: Take an umbrella because it may rain.
items.note: Carry an umbrella when taking it with you; hold an umbrella when using it open.

items.example: He is carrying a suitcase at the station.
items.note: A suitcase is a travel bag, typically carried or wheeled rather than worn.

items.example: She is carrying a handbag to the office.
items.note: A handbag is a bag carried by a person. The word also appears as a compound-noun exercise target in Unit 03.

items.example: My clothes are clean and dry.
items.note: Clothes is a plural noun: my clothes are dry. For one item, say a piece of clothing or an item of clothing.

items.example: I get dressed in the morning before breakfast.
items.note: This routine expression can be expanded with specific actions, such as putting on socks or shoes.
